items.readme_text:
# VIctory fork (work in progress)

A work-in-progress fork of [VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory), a
compatibility layer that runs an Xbox Series title natively on Windows from
files the user supplies. This fork follows upstream
`main` and adds fixes aimed at one goal: getting the game's world to render
correctly and playably on one particular PC.

**This repository contains no game files, code or assets.** You need your own
copy of the game. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's
developer or publisher.

## Credits

- **[VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory)** by Marvisak and its
  contributors is the base of everything here: the loader, the runtime
  services, the Direct3D 12 back end and the shader recompiler. Licensed
  GPL-3.0-or-later; so is this fork. Upstream's history is kept intact below
  the single commit that carries this fork's changes.
- **[XCL](https://github.com/ivall/xcl)** by ivall and its contributors
  (GPL-2.0-only) was used as a reference for how the same title behaves under
  another layer. Fixes inspired by it were written anew in VIctory's code.
- The guard over every view of a memory page is code by **myokex**
  ([victory-amd](https://github.com/myokex/victory-amd), commit `c6dc4d8`), which
  adapts pull request #115 here by Spexivus, its correction by joroyt and a part of
  VIctory #1122 by tightfall. The read-beside fix for kernel reads into title
  memory is by **Joshua Odom** (commit `10ea38e` of the same fork family). Both
  are carried here unchanged apart from one merge conflict.
- This fork's changes were developed with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code).

## Status of this fork (2026-11-25)

**Not playable yet: 2.5 to 4 frames per second, and shadowed areas are black.**
Tested on one machine: Windows 11, Intel i7-14700KF, NVIDIA RTX 4070 12 GB,
32 GB RAM. The Series X profile is used throughout.

| Stage | State in this fork |
|-------|--------------------|
| Boot, menus, start screen | works, 30 fps (as upstream) |
| Opening cutscene | plays from start to finish, in order, lit: title cards, credits cards, night and dusk shots |
| Saves | the game autosaves a checkpoint and loads it again |
| First gameplay scene (the prologue) | renders: characters, textures, sky, sunlit exterior; HUD, pause menu and pad input work |
| Light in shadow | missing: the game's ray-traced bounce light and ray-traced lamp and sun shadows do not run yet, so anything the sun does not hit directly is black |
| Frame rate in the world | 2-4 fps: 420-450 ms per frame by default, 240-350 ms with the newer switches (`VICTORY_RELAY=2`, or `VICTORY_LATE_WAIT=3 VICTORY_WIDE_BACK=1 VICTORY_CARD_BUFFERS_MIN_MB=1 VICTORY_CARD_BUFFERS_MB=1024`); it started at 3-6 seconds per frame |
| Stability | no driver hang or device loss in normal runs (a hang introduced by the wave64 update was found and fixed: its barrier form for 64-lane programs is now off unless `VICTORY_WAVE_WIDE=1`) |

### Newest (2026-11-25, evening UTC)

**Update, 2026-11-25 evening: a frame capture built into the layer, and a
card time that does not add up yet.** No frame-rate gain is claimed; the
headline numbers stand. (A heavier view of the first room: 122 ms a frame
at 6,774 draws in run 266. The 97 to 104 ms below are at about 3,850
draws.) This push is the README only: the code is not in this tree yet.
- **An outside frame debugger did not work here.** RenderDoc 1.45, loaded
  through a hook (`VICTORY_RENDERDOC=<path of its DLL>`), ended run 263
  after about 10 s of loading: an access violation inside its library,
  then "device suspended" from every host call (its wrapped device; no
  driver event). The stack showed a streaming program's capture hook
  making a Direct3D 11-on-12 device on the wrapped device. A MISTAKE of
  that run: the driver refused the saved pipeline library and the layer
  saved an empty one over it (366 MB of 3,385 pipelines became 32 bytes;
  the next run drew black frames at 0.7 to 1.5 frames a second while
  building them again). Fixed: a rejected library is kept as
  `host-pipelines.rejected.bin`, never saved over, and with RenderDoc
  loaded the library is neither read nor saved.
- **DirectStorage reads wait for the title's Submit** (after upstream
  VIctory eddde734: its hold and two tests, not its diagnostics). The
  title fills a batch's page list only right before its Submit; a queue
  that sent itself when half full started reads into physical pages
  before that. Run 266: 3 such cases (2,079 reads held of a queue of
  4,159), no stall, 0 failed page writes, frame time not worse. Faces
  were right in that one launch; face faults come and go between
  launches, so a cure is not shown yet.
- **Processor use, per core and per thread (runs 266, 267): nothing is
  full.** Of 28 logical processors the machine keeps 6.7 busy in the
  cutscene and 4.5 in the room, the process about 3.6 and 3.1. The
  busiest thread, the layer's submit thread, is 42 to 58 % busy; the
  title's most crowded pinned group is 25 to 29 % full. No look in the
  room found the render, the submit or a recording thread on a slow core
  (0 of 1, 0 of 8, 0 of 120). `VICTORY_SPREAD=alt` in the cutscene: 262 ms
  a frame off, 262 on. The frame is a chain of waits: more cores alone
  give nothing. Splitting the submit thread's work would use them: it
  works 83 ms of the room's 122 ms frame (bound: a frame of about 100).
- **`VICTORY_WIDE_REFRESH=alt`: no gain, dropped** (copies of title memory
  refreshed on several threads, twenty seconds on, twenty off). Cutscene,
  run 268: copies 31.2 -> 26.0 ms a frame (17 %) where 10 to 15 ms were
  predicted. Room, run 269, 10 readings each way: copies 30.6 ms off, 34.1
  on; submit thread 78.6 against 78.4 ms.
- **Frame shot: a capture of one frame, built into the layer**
  (`VICTORY_SHOT=<folder>`; taken when a file named `take` appears there,
  or at `VICTORY_SHOT_AT=<frames after the first frame of 500 draws>`). A
  shot holds every command of the frame in order (draws, dispatches,
  copies, submissions, with list and thread), the card's clock before
  each command, and a picture of each texture as a pass leaves it. It
  loads no DLL and wraps no device: only texture read-backs and
  timestamps, which every run uses already. Hence built in, not outside.
- With little memory free, a shot takes at most half of what is free
  above 0.7 GB, and pictures that do not fit are taken in parts from
  later frames. A shot is exactly one frame of the title: the title
  records its next frame while the layer still runs this one, and the
  first form (run 269) held both, so every pass showed twice. It also
  took 0 pictures: the title uses enhanced barriers and the layer moves
  textures between states itself; the pictures are now taken there.
- First shots, run 270 (300 s, 0 errors, no driver event), both in the
  opening cutscene. Frame 1864: 6,348 lines, 3,618 draws and dispatches,
  54 pictures of 82 places, then ended early with 685 MB free. Frame
  2849, complete: 10,334 lines, 7,120 draws and dispatches, 77 of 78
  pictures. Those looked at are right pictures of the frame.
- **What the shots say, and what is NOT explained.** Run 270's two
  frames: the card's time for the title's own commands is 20.1 ms
  (compute 13.3, drawing 6.3) and 22.0 ms (drawing 11.3, compute 10.1).
  The older per-list card meter gives the title's lists 57 to 78 ms a
  frame at that time: 35 to 55 ms more. The shot then got a stamp at
  every list's start and around the layer's own lists. Run 271's two
  frames: the title's commands 25.2 and 15.4 ms; the layer's
  send-and-hash lists 35.0 and 17.8 ms (14 and 8 lists), its compare
  lists 12.1 and 6.3 ms (13 and 7). The lists it runs before title lists
  took 36.1 ms in the second frame, but they also hold the shot's own
  picture copies, not separated yet: the gap is not accounted for. If it
  is the layer's, the card's ceiling is higher than the "near 20 frames
  a second" given below, which rests on the per-list meter.
- **The staging-buffer pool, on and off in turn** (run 270,
  `VICTORY_STAGING_POOL=alt`, 128 MB kept). On by default; off in test
  runs since run 224, its first long run, lost the device (cause never
  found; that driver error had also come up before the pool existed).
  Predicted: page faults per texture upload from about 100 to well under
  50, long frames 60 to 115 ms shorter at equal uploads. Measured: 6.27
  frames a second off, 5.77 on (different scenes; the 7 pairs go both
  ways). Long frames average 391 ms with 204 uploads off, 421 ms with 310
  on: 1.92 ms an upload off, 1.36 on, but the texture pass fills its 250
  ms time budget either way, so frames are no shorter. Page faults per
  upload: 132.7 off, 128.9 on: prediction not met. No gain shown: not
  adopted. The frame log's "staging made" counter read 0 with the pool
  off; it counts now.
- **Memory, measured.** The process holds about 24 GB, 16 GB of it in
  memory, on a 32 GB PC. Free: 3.6 GB in the cutscene and 0.9 to 1.8 GB
  in the room in run 269; 3.6 to 5.3 GB late in run 270 (why they differ
  is not known). The card is nearly full: 9.0 of a 10.2 GB budget. Title
  buffers of 1 MiB and more are in its memory in these runs (1,024 MB at
  most); the 872 copies of what the title's own allocator hands out
  (vertices, indices, constants: 3.6 GB) are in the PC's memory and read
  over the bus at every draw. The card has no room for all of them: it
  would come out of the textures' share.
- **Some of those copies in the card's memory: fewer long frames, in two
  launches of two** (`VICTORY_CARD_WINDOWS_MB`, off by default). Run 271
  asked for 512 MB (124 to 137 copies went to the card), run 272 for
  2,048 MB (355 copies, 1,356 MB, went there; the layer's own line at 80 %
  of the card's budget turned the rest down). Both: 300 s, 0 errors, no
  driver event, pictures right. Frames a second in three stretches of the
  opening cutscene (20 to 110 s, 110 to 200 s, 200 to 290 s after its
  first frame), and the share of the last stretch's time spent in frames
  over 250 ms:

  | run | on the card | first | middle | last | long frames, last stretch |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 269 | none | 3.95 | 7.49 | 7.59 | 21 % |
  | 270 | none | 3.93 | 7.99 | 6.68 | 26 % |
  | 271 | 512 MB | 5.44 | 7.26 | 8.48 | 4 % |
  | 272 | 1,356 MB | 5.42 | 8.16 | 8.32 | 6 % |

  Textures made again after being let go for lack of room: 5.1 and 6.9 GB
  in the runs without, 1.9 and 1.1 GB with. That is what the long frames
  are made of. Why fewer textures are let go is not known: the title's
  draws cost the card the same per command with and without (+1 %, 37
  shader sets found in both captures). The price: passes that made no
  texture for lack of room rose (2,067 and 1,280 without; 2,504 and 3,699
  with). Four launches, two each way, and earlier launches without it
  reached 3.4 to 5.1 in the first stretch: a result, not yet a default.
- A review of the open pull requests for frame rate found no single large
  gain. The nearest is #1014 (the card-side compare hashes a piece with
  64 threads; a tester's claim on an RTX 4080: send-and-hash lists 14.0
  -> 2.5 ms, compare lists 5.6 -> 1.3 ms). Not measured here.
- **Next, none of it measured yet:** (1) the shot's own copies taken out
  of the lists the layer runs before title lists, so the card's frame
  adds up; (2) those copies as one buffer in a GPU upload heap (the
  card's memory written directly by the processor through a resizable
  BAR), with no second copy in the PC's memory and no pass that sends it
  up: written, not built; (3) what shaders wrote left on the card until
  the title's processor reads it, where today every changed piece is
  fetched back every frame (42 to 70 MB): being studied, nothing built;
  (4) a faster byte compare for the submit thread (8 and 64 bytes at a
  time; its test of 20,000 cases against the byte-by-byte walk passes;
  not in a run yet); (5) the texture pass's time budget, 250 ms against
  less, in turn inside one run (written, not built). Title buffers in
  place (`VICTORY_INPLACE`) were listed as the large step; a closer look
  at this PC says otherwise: both ways of opening title memory to the
  card pin it in a PC with 1 to 5 GB free, and the buffer that carries
  the most traffic cannot be opened at all. A memory step and a modest
  time step, not the road to 30 frames a second by itself.

### Earlier (up to 2026-11-25 afternoon)

**Update, 2026-11-25 afternoon: what a frame is made of, measured, and two
changes that hold.** First rooms, about 3,850 draws a frame: 104 ms a frame
(9.6 frames a second) with the first two changes below, 97 ms (10.3)
with all of them, from about 120 ms in the morning. Still far from the console's 33 ms.
- How the title paces itself (new meters in `fence.rs` and
  `console_insn.rs`): it never asks for an event. Each frame begins with
  one small submission and a signal, and a title thread then waits for
  that fence value by reading it in memory with `monitorx` / `mwaitx`
  (AMD-only: about 280,000 emulated exceptions a second on an Intel
  processor, all from this wait). The value is set when the layer has
  finished the whole frame before. So a frame is the time the layer needs
  for one frame's burst of submissions plus about 20 ms of the title's
  own; putting presents behind the line, or giving the title's threads
  more processors, changes nothing (both measured).
- Two walls stand side by side and both are full: the layer's submit
  thread (about 95 ms of a 120 ms frame in the morning) and the card
  (about 102 ms busy, by a timestamp pair around every host list:
  `cardmeter.rs`). Taking time off one alone moved the frame by 0 to 7 %.
- `VICTORY_JOIN_PARTS=1` (off by default): the title's lists wait for
  memory values, which cut its ~15 submissions a frame into ~29 parts;
  parts that follow one another now go to the host as one submission
  (9 a frame), the same lists in the same order. About 6 %.
- `VICTORY_BACK_OWN_VIEW=1` (off by default): what shaders wrote goes
  back into title view memory through a view of the layer's own, so the
  copy that wrote it is not read in again. About 9 % (submit thread 93 ->
  81 ms a frame, 104 -> 80 MB a frame checked). A CORRECTION: an earlier
  run seemed to show washed-out frames with this switch; the same frames
  turn up in about 6 of 21 runs with no switch at all (cause not known),
  and `VICTORY_BACK_OWN_CHECK=1` counted 0 stores gone astray in 1.36
  million.
- Where the card's time goes now (`VICTORY_CARD_METER_PIPELINES=1`, a
  table by pipeline): no pass is large. About 82 ms of the title's lists
  are spread over ~3,400 pipeline bindings a frame; ~2,400 of the
  indirect commands still get a clamp pass of the layer's with draw
  windows on (960 are compute dispatches; about 1,000 are mesh records
  the title keeps scattered through a 100 MB argument buffer, which a
  window of records at one step cannot serve).
- `VICTORY_INDIRECT_GATHER=1` (off by default): a single indirect record
  that misses its window gets a slot in a scratch buffer of its list, and
  the list's prelude clamps all such records in one pass by a table of
  their offsets (the clamp shader with a gather bit), where each draw had
  a compute pass of the layer's in front of it. Proved by clamping every
  gathered record again at its draw and comparing on the card
  (`VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW_CHECK=1`): 7.9 million records, none differed.
  About 600 of the ~1,600 draws that missed a window are served; the
  others come after a dispatch or a storing draw in their list. With
  `VICTORY_CARD_REHASH_RUNS=1`: 104 -> 97 ms a frame (10.3 frames a
  second at 3,800 draws).
- What the card's time is now, added up: of ~87 ms busy in a 97 ms
  frame, the layer's own lists are ~19 ms and its clamp passes 10-20 ms;
  about 50 ms are the title's own ~30 compute passes and its geometry at
  2560x1440 as translated. With every pass of the layer's gone, this
  scene would still be near 20 frames a second on this card: the
  translated shaders have to get cheaper too. (Open again: see the evening update above.)
- The frame rate is drawn into the top left corner of every frame shown
  (`fpsbox.rs`; `VICTORY_FPS_COUNTER=0`: not): the window's caption has
  it too, but a capture of the picture does not carry the caption.
- `VICTORY_COPY_CHANGED=1` (off by default): a refresh of a copy in the
  card's memory sends on only the 256-byte chunks that differ from the
  copy's CPU side. The layer's sync lists on the card fall from 12 to 8
  ms a frame, the submit thread pays 3.6 ms for the compare and is then
  the limit: no net gain yet.
- HONEST LIMIT OF ALL THE ABOVE: those numbers are the scene standing
  still. While the camera moves the title streams assets, and about half
  the time goes to frames of ~490 ms in which the card is idle for ~330
  ms: some 850 remaps of title memory, 260 texture uploads and 450 disk
  reads in one frame. That is the next thing to measure and cut.
- The dips while moving, measured (a sampling profile of the opening
  cutscene, and a 370 s play session): the mean is 4.5 frames a second,
  with half the time in frames of ~490 ms in which the card is idle for
  ~330 ms. In those frames the title's render thread waits for its own
  jobs, not for the layer. One of those jobs is the title's page-mapping
  copies (`CopyPageMappingsBatchX` -> `xmem::map_alias`): the title maps
  every streamed texture page into its tiled heap, a range of one page
  each (over 4,096 different pool pages in a minute, about 850 pages in
  a frame that streams), and each is a view taken away and a view mapped
  in the kernel: 32 ms of every cutscene frame, 246 ms of a streaming
  frame, nearly all of it waiting on the process's address space.
- Two attempts on that, both taken back out: leaving alone pages that
  already show what is asked (counted: there are none, every remap is a
  real change), and mapping pool pages in a row as one view (1.8 to 4.2
  pages a view, remap time 140 -> 79 ms a frame, BUT faces came out black
  or red and one run drew garbage in 3 launches of 3, against none in 6
  launches without it). Reverted; why a longer view breaks texture
  streaming is not known yet.
- Measured and found to give nothing (switches left in, off):
  `VICTORY_REFRESH_ONCE`, `VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT`, `VICTORY_VIEW_KNOWN`,
  `VICTORY_SPREAD`, `VICTORY_QUEUE2=3`, `VICTORY_WINDOW_JUMP`. Each has an
  `=alt` form (twenty seconds on, twenty off, each change said in the
  log) so that one run measures both in the same scene.

**Update, the same night: the first room now renders right on the test
machine** (walls, textures, people, lamps), at 190 to 450 ms a frame (2 to 5
frames a second): the picture work has caught up, the frame rate has not.
What did it, on top of the list below:
- Descriptor records the title copies into its heap as plain bytes are
  mirrored before every submission (pull request #305 by Flyander, after
  upstream VIctory 86a5ed6). Measured here: about 40,000 records a frame
  that no call had announced; their host slots were empty or stale.
- A buffer view that does not start on an element of its buffer's host
  copy gets a copy of its own bytes instead of being refused (after
  upstream 86a5ed6): 3 to 6 such views a frame.
- Room on the card is kept for the render targets and buffer copies a
  world makes in its first frame: 98 buffer copies are made (945 MB) where
  the runs before made 1, and the processor no longer compares 550 to
  710 MB a frame looking for shader writes (25 MB now).
- Levels on demand ran on the card for the first time
  (`VICTORY_LEVELS_ON_DEMAND=1`, still off by default; with the fixes of
  pull request #747 by AscilCH): 3.1 GB of the card not allocated for
  texture levels the title does not hold, no device loss.
- Guarded blocks under storage writes are opened by default; 14 more
  shader programs translate; a program is translated with first-half
  interpolation pairs only if it was refused for one (with that on for
  every program, 8,551 working pixel programs came out changed).
- Frame rate, first cuts on the processor side: the descriptor sync uses a
  cheap fingerprint and leaves draw-table slots to their draws (the pass
  over the heap went from 70-220 ms a frame to about 3), and memory the
  guards already hold is not asked of the write watch (pull request #670
  by Jonirulah). Card copies' pieces can come down inside their own
  flights (pull request #648 by Jonirulah, `VICTORY_CARD_FETCH_INFLIGHT=1`,
  off by default: the copy-back thread's wait went from 181 ms a frame to
  0 here, but the card got busier, so no gain is claimed yet). The frame is
  still 250 to 380 ms: the card is the limit now, most of it the
  per-record clamp before each of some 6,700 indirect draws a frame.
- Pull request #220 (cheaper indirect draws) is IN this tree now, its
  windows off by default (`VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW=1`). History, so nobody
  repeats it: with windows on it lost the device three times here. Its own
  checker (`VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW_CHECK=1`) then showed one list drawing
  90 records of 2^24 vertices from a window, where the per-draw path lets
  eight through; a record of 2^23 vertices an instance or more now runs
  empty. Since that fix: eight runs with windows on, seven without a
  device loss and one that lost the device 44 s into the world (cause not
  found; see the driver watch below). One earlier loss after the fix had
  the in-flight fetch (#648) on as well; do not combine the two. The
  in-flight fetch itself measured slower here in two runs and stays off.
- Frame rate, second night (an RTX 4070; the first room went from about
  3.5-4 to 6-7 frames a second with ALL of the switches below; the
  defaults are unchanged and give about 4.5-5):
  - `VICTORY_ASYNC_SUBMIT=1`: submissions are prepared and sent by a
    thread of the layer, not by the title's render thread, which a
    profile showed inside the submit path for 257 of 292 ms a frame.
  - `VICTORY_QUEUE2=1`: fetches of what shaders wrote go to a copy queue
    (brought back, with the fix for a piece fetched beside a later
    flight); the copy-back thread's wait fell from about 125 to 7 ms a
    frame.
  - `VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW=1`: see above.
  - `VICTORY_TEXTURE_NO_WAIT=1`: a texture refresh no longer waits while
    the title remaps memory; the loading phase had 5 readings over a
    second where it had 18.
  - `VICTORY_MERGE_GAP=64 VICTORY_MERGE_RUNS=4096`: title bytes put in
    under flights' shader writes are joined over small gaps (NOT exact:
    read the comment at `merge_gap` before using it).
  - On by default: fills of upload memory and read-only buffer copies no
    longer wait for flights and are checked against what the flights then
    wrote (`VICTORY_FILL_WAIT=1` waits as before; no mismatch in any run
    so far); up to 512 idle host lists and texture staging buffers are
    reused instead of made and freed every frame.
  - `VICTORY_PROFILE=1` (diagnostics builds): a sampling profiler inside
    the layer; it is how the above was found.
- Frame rate, third session: measuring first (same RTX 4070, first room).
  - A frame log (`VICTORY_FRAME_LOG`, on in diagnostics builds): every
    frame's length, and for the usual frame and each long one what it was
    made of (the render thread's time in the present call, the submit
    thread's work, copies, copy-back, recording, texture work, faults,
    disk). A card meter (`VICTORY_CARD_METER`) adds the card's time by
    kind of list from a timestamp at each list's start and end.
  - What they showed, windows off: a usual frame of 136 ms; the title's
    render thread waits 77 ms of it in the present call for the submit
    thread, which works 118 ms (copies of title memory 41, copy-back 40);
    the card is 85-98 % busy, of about 130 ms a frame 16 ms in our lists
    that bring card copies up to date, 10 ms in our compare lists and 102
    ms in the title's own lists with the per-record clamp. Frame time is
    linear in draws (about 32 microseconds a draw all-in): the title draws
    about twice as much on some frames, which are the long ones.
  - The regular dips of earlier test runs were the test harness: a saved
    frame (`VICTORY_CAPTURE_WORLD`, every 8th world frame) is read back
    and written as a PNG inside the present, 235 ms each.
    `VICTORY_CAPTURE_WORLD_EVERY=64` for runs that measure speed.
  - `VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW=1` measured again with those instruments. A
    CORRECTION: the first figures given here (6.0 against 8.9 frames a
    second) compared two runs that stood in different scenes during the
    measured window (about 4,300 against 1,550 draws a frame) and are
    withdrawn. Compared at equal draws, by a line fitted to each run's
    frame times against its draws per frame: windows off 145 ms at 4,500
    draws and 271 ms at 10,000; windows on with `VICTORY_COPY_PLAIN=1`
    124 ms and 211 ms. On screen: 7-8 frames a second in the first rooms,
    10-12 in their lighter views.
  - A driver watch (on by default; `VICTORY_DRIVER_WATCH=0` off): the
    layer subscribes to the system's event log and logs every entry of a
    display driver as it is recorded; the first one turns draw windows
    off for the rest of the run. Every device loss here had such entries
    2.7 to 55 seconds before the device was removed, and no run without
    them lost its device.
  - A copy between two title textures that share one host texture is no
    longer recorded (the host does not allow a texture copied onto
    itself): 402 of them in a five-minute run.
  - The list of shader-visible heaps is a reader-writer lock (recording
    threads waited 48 ms a frame, summed, behind the heap sync); the heap
    sync looks at a changed page's records under one lock, fingerprint
    first; guarded view memory is left out of a submission's write-watch
    askings ahead (after triippywhale).
  - `VICTORY_COPY_PLAIN=1`: copies of title memory made in place by this
    process, with a handler that falls back to the kernel's copy on a
    missing page. Its first form also took the layer's one-byte "is this
    page there" reads, 1,000 to 1,300 faults a frame, and won nothing;
    reads under 256 bytes now stay with the kernel and a source that
    faulted is left alone for two seconds (4 to 9 faults a frame). The
    submit thread's kernel time fell from 44 to 20 ms a frame; the
    picture is the same.
  - The layer's submit and copy-back threads ask for the fast cores of a
    hybrid processor (`VICTORY_FAST_CORES=0`: not): the submit thread was
    found on a slow core in 6 % of its looks, now in none of 21,059.
    `VICTORY_DISK_CORES=slow` (off, not measured) asks the slow cores for
    the DirectStorage workers, which are as many as the logical
    processors and free to run anywhere.
  - Behind switches, built and unit-tested, not yet shown to pay:
    `VICTORY_REFRESH_ONCE=1`, `VICTORY_VIEW_KNOWN=1`,
    `VICTORY_BACK_OWN_VIEW=1` (picture to be checked),
    `VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT=1` (the present goes behind the queue's line;
    no gain while the card is the limit).
  - Tried and refused: `VICTORY_BVH_HOLD=1` holds back the 64 programs
    that walk ray-tracing structures nothing has built; the picture loses
    its indirect light with it, so it stays off.
  - The process opts out of the system's efficiency mode
    (`VICTORY_EFFICIENCY_MODE=1` leaves it); on a hybrid processor the
    frame log found the title's render and recording threads on fast
    cores in every look of a run, and the layer's submit thread on a slow
    core in 6 % of its looks.
  Still open: the per-record clamp is most of the card's time, and the
  copies between the PC's memory and the card's are most of the submit
  thread's; the cause of the one device loss with windows is not known.
  A first play session past the first rooms reached the open world and
  lost the device there with no driver entry (reason "device removed"):
  the card had no room for new textures from the opening cutscene on
  (9.2 of a 10.3 GB budget on a 12 GB card; 2,073 passes made no texture
  for lack of room; 44,613 textures let go and made again in 13 minutes).
  Cause of that removal not known either.
- Known and counted, not fixed yet: an indirect compute pass asks for
  about 77,500 thread groups in x where one dispatch runs 65,535 (the
  rest is cut off).

Memory sync between the title's memory and the copies on the card:
- **A write through one view of a physical page is seen by the copies taken
  through its other views** (`VICTORY_VIEW_GUARD=0` turns it off). The title
  shows one page at several addresses and a copy was guarded at one of them
  only. Measured on the test machine: 0.8 to 1.0 million such writes in a
  five-minute run, every one of which used to leave a copy stale. Since it
  went in, the first room had its walls in the later frames of 4 runs out of
  4 (2 of 5 before); the room's very first shot still comes up without walls
  in some runs.
- Kernel reads into title memory are read beside and copied in, so a block
  guarded again in between no longer fails the read.
- Writes of the storage layer into physical pages are counted where the title
  has those pages mapped (10,000 to 50,000 guarded blocks of copies lay under
  them in every run) and can open the guards there:
  `VICTORY_PAGE_WRITES=guards` (off by default; `1`, `slots`, `all` do more).
- Failed page-destination reads are retried (`VICTORY_DSTORAGE_RETRIES=0` = as before).

Card memory (the test card is full from the first frame of the world: 85 to
99 % of its budget for a whole run, about 26,000 texture copies let go and
3,400 made again in five minutes, 2.8 GB of render targets that are all in
use):
- Levels on demand, **off by default** (`VICTORY_LEVELS_ON_DEMAND=1`): a
  texture the title fills takes card memory only for the levels the title
  holds (2.2 to 3.0 GB of the copies were levels it does not hold). Its test
  runs on the software adapter; it has not run on a card yet.
- Refused texture slots are held back for a few seconds so that a pass
  reaches the slots behind them (`VICTORY_FULL_CARD_PASS=0` = as before);
  room can be kept for the card copies of title buffers
  (`VICTORY_CARD_ROOM_FOR_BUFFERS=1`, off).

Tools and diagnostics:
- `victory translate <shader file> --warm all --jobs N` translates every
  shader ahead of a run, on the processor only (about 4.5 to 6.5 minutes
  here); the shader cache is keyed on the translator's source, so a new
  build that does not touch the translator starts warm.
- Counters, all off or diagnostics-only: `VICTORY_MERGE_RACE=1` (title bytes
  a copy-back is about to put back to older values: none found in 138,000
  copy-backs), `VICTORY_WALLS_TRACE`, `VICTORY_CARD_ACCOUNTING`, and a census
  of the copies the texture sweep never lets go.

### What this fork changed (summary)

Rendering:
- Meshlet culling read its scene buffers as the wrong kind of view, so the world drew almost nothing; fixed.
- Per-draw descriptor tables could run out, after which draws used slots never made for them and the card hung; fixed.
- Light packed by the game's compute shaders was read back through empty copies (sky, probes, fog); fixed for every mip level and layer.
- The fog reconstruction, shadow-mask, hair, blend-shape skinning, fire and several material programs did not translate; fixed.
- Gathers at a named mip level (with and without an offset) read level 0; fixed.
- Implicit-level samples outside pixel shaders produced invalid DXIL in 730 compute programs; fixed.
- Rectangle lists, depth and stencil twins for depth textures written by compute, texture read-backs.
- Ray tracing, in progress and off by default: the game's own structure-builder programs translate, title memory can be read by raw address from shaders, the hardware ray/box and ray/triangle test is emulated in DXIL (checked against a reference on the GPU), and 59 of the 64 trace programs translate. Nothing is lit by it yet. See [docs/fork-ray-tracing.md](docs/fork-ray-tracing.md).

Speed and memory:
- Waits for memory values, write-watch queries and page queries no longer walk page tables per call.
- Large title buffers get a copy in card memory, with shader writes found by hashing on the card.
- Submissions can be sent ahead of the wait for the card (`VICTORY_LATE_WAIT`), with a relay thread that lands results as the card finishes (`VICTORY_RELAY`): in a first five-minute run the card's idle time behind the submitting thread fell from about 136 to 30 ms per frame.
- Title memory can be opened as a graphics heap so that buffers are used in place instead of copied (`VICTORY_INPLACE`, first stage only; a probe confirmed the approach on the test GPU).
- The bindless texture queue no longer uploads stale views; the view table no longer grows without bound; the pipeline library is mapped instead of read into memory.
- An intermittent device loss was traced to the pipeline library file being replaced while mapped; fixed.

- Translated shaders get clean-up passes over the finished module (dead code, constant folding, reuse of values, branch facts); the pack's host instruction count falls by about 43 %, worth about 20 ms of GPU time per frame on the test machine (`VICTORY_SHADER_OPT=0` turns them off).

Most of the newer speed changes sit behind environment switches that are off
by default (`VICTORY_LATE_WAIT`, `VICTORY_RELAY`, `VICTORY_WIDE_BACK`,
`VICTORY_CARD_BUFFERS_MIN_MB`, `VICTORY_INPLACE`, `VICTORY_BVH_BUILDER`, ...).
Each is described in a comment where it is read.

### Known problems

- Everything in shadow is black (see above).
- The interior of the first gameplay room is sometimes not drawn after the cutscene hands over to gameplay.
- Around 24 GB of memory is in use during play, about 16 GB of it in memory: the 32 GB test PC has about 1 to 5 GB free, and the 12 GB card is nearly full, so textures are let go and made again for lack of room.
- A few style lints are switched off for this fork in the workspace `Cargo.toml` until the newer code is tidied.
- Many changes here are specific to this title and this GPU, and some are marked `shortcut:` in the code where they approximate what the console does.

Everything below this line is upstream VIctory's own README, unchanged; its
status section describes upstream, not this fork.

# VIctory

Runs the title (Xbox Series X|S) natively on Windows, from files
the user supplies.

The title's x86-64 code runs unchanged inside our process; VIctory supplies
the platform underneath it and converts the title's data, ahead of time where
it can and on first use where it must (shaders). See
[docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

## Status (2026-11-23)

**Not playable yet.** The title boots, runs its menus at its own 30 fps and
loads the world, where rendering fails.

| Stage | State |
|-------|-------|
| Boot, first-boot screens (accessibility, language, settings, legal) | works, 30 fps |
| Intro video with sound | works |
| Start screen, profile and saves | works |
| Loading into the world (about 50 s) | works |
| The world (first mission's intro) | reached and runs with indirect draws; its title card renders, the scene after it is still dark; 0.5-1.8 s per frame |

Tested on one machine: Windows 11, AMD RX 6700 XT.

> **Warning.** Entering the world on a real GPU can currently hang it, and
> Windows then resets the display driver (every monitor goes black for a
> moment). To look further, use a diagnostics build with
> `VICTORY_D3D12_WARP=1`, which renders on the software adapter.

What each part does today and what it still needs:

| Subsystem | Today | Needs |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| Loader | Runs the title's executable and its DLLs in our process; crash reports name the faulting code and are kept in `crashes.log` | – |
| Runtime services | One signed-in offline user, licences, packages, saves that survive a kill at any step, text entry dialog | Speech is silent; the dialog and relaunch are untested live |
| Network | Offline by design: the title cannot reach the network | – |
| Files and streaming | Archives and streamed data read, zlib and BCPack decoded in parallel | Loading is limited by writes into title memory |
| Input | XInput pads, keyboard, keyboard stand-in pad | Trigger rumble |
| Audio | Menu, video and loading sound; XMA voices and Opus streams decode | Reverb is silent; Opus results unverified against the title |
| GPU: menus | Draws, compute and presentation on host D3D12; only changed title memory is copied | Frame pacing drifts on one screen in release builds |
| GPU: world | Mesh pipelines, shader-written buffers, descriptor lifetimes, indirect execution (arguments clamped), pipelines made by worker threads and kept on disk | Most of the scene is still missing (untranslated shaders drop draws); frames take seconds; real queries, depth bounds, HDR and scaling are missing |
| Shaders | Console GPU code recompiled to DXIL at first use, cached on disk. Menus: all. World: mesh 8,191 of 8,506, vertex/pixel 10,617 of 12,346, compute 1,643 of 2,539 | 64-bit image atomics, merged geometry stages, the ray-tracing builder's shaders; some compute programs need a GPU with 64-lane waves |
| Textures | Console tiled layouts and detiling for the modes the title uses | Render-target metadata planes |
| Series S mode | Runs through the menus to the loading screen | The world, as above |

## Getting started

Requirements: Windows 10/11 x64, a CPU with AVX2, a Direct3D 12 GPU with
shader model 6.6 (and mesh shaders for the world), Rust (pinned in
`rust-toolchain.toml`).

The title also needs several GiB of available Windows commit at startup.
Check **Committed** under **Task Manager → Performance → Memory**. If
`crashes.log` reports Windows error 1455, close other applications or increase
the Windows paging file size, then retry.

```powershell
cargo xtask install-hooks                # asset-policy check on every commit
copy victory.example.toml victory.toml   # then set your paths (outside the repo)
cargo test --workspace                   # needs no game data
cargo run -p victory -- config           # check your paths
```

Run the title:

```powershell
cargo build --release -p victory
target\release\victory.exe run <game dir>\<the title's exe> --execute
```

The window caption shows the framerate. Saves, settings and `crashes.log`
are kept under the data folder (default `%LOCALAPPDATA%\victory\data`), derived
data under the cache folder.

Input: XInput pads. With none connected the keyboard is a pad while the
title's window has focus:

| Keys | Pad |
|------|-----|
| W A S D / I J K L | left / right stick |
| arrows | D-pad |
| Enter, Backspace, X, Y | A, B, X, Y |
| Q / E, Z / C | shoulders, triggers |
| F / H | stick clicks |
| Esc, Tab | Menu, View |

## Commands

```
victory inspect <exe|dll> [--imports] [--exports]
victory census [paths...] [--missing] [--strict]
victory lib-exports <import.lib> [--list]
victory shader-info [paths...] [--verbose] [--disasm]
victory translate [paths...] [--validate] [--pipelines] [--list] [--jobs N]
victory run <exe> [--execute] [--unimplemented trap|zero] [--strict]
            [--console series-x|series-s] [-- <title arguments>]
victory config
```

Logging: `VICTORY_LOG=victory_loader=trace,info` (a release build logs
info and above).

## Debugging

A release build has no debugging aids. Build them in with

```powershell
cargo build --profile diag -p victory --features diagnostics   # target\diag\victory.exe
```

| Variable | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| `VICTORY_LOG=<target>=debug,...` | debug and trace output |
| `VICTORY_STACKS=20,60` | every thread's stack at those seconds |
| `VICTORY_WATCH=<rva>,...` | logs a title u32 when it changes |
| `VICTORY_KEYS=30:Enter,35:X` | presses keys at those seconds, focus or not |
| `VICTORY_CRASH_SAVE=<rva>:<len>,...` | saves title memory to the cache folder on a crash |
| `VICTORY_CAPTURE=<dir>` | saves presented frames (powers of two, or `VICTORY_CAPTURE_FRAMES=<list>`) |
| `VICTORY_DUMP_TARGETS=1` | with the two above, saves every render target of those frames |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_DEBUG=1` | host debug layer |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_GBV=1` | with the above, GPU-based validation (bad descriptor use reported, not faulted; slow) |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_DRED=1` | on a GPU failure, the allocation hit and the commands in flight |
| `VICTORY_PIPELINE_WAIT_MS=24` | reduce the per-frame wait for background pipeline creation from the default of 500 ms. A draw can be omitted until its pipeline is ready |
| `VICTORY_SKIP_PIPELINES=<hash>,...` | omit draws and dispatches, including indirect ones, whose pipeline contains a listed 16-digit shader hash |
| `VICTORY_GPU_TIMING=1` | with the above, each list of a submission run and timed on its own; slow lists logged with their slowest commands |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_WARP=1` | host device on the software adapter (slow; cannot reset the driver) |
| `VICTORY_SHADER_LOOP_LIMIT=<n>` | translated shader loops stop after `n` iterations per lane instead of 2^20 (own shader cache entries); if a lower `n` makes world frames much faster, loops hitting the limit are what makes them slow |
| `VICTORY_AUDIO_CAPTURE=<file.wav>` | records what the title plays (our process only) |
| `VICTORY_XMA_DUMP=<dir>` | saves the first 32 XMA voices' context and input |

Every build appends crashes and host GPU failures to `crashes.log` in the
title's data folder.

It encodes proven patterns and methodologies refined through automated generation processes. The playbook distills key insights from successfully building all 18 diverse, production-ready harnesses. ### Critical Lessons | Lesson | Description | |--------|-------------| | **Use the real software** | The CLI MUST call the actual application for rendering. No Pillow replacements for GIMP, no custom renderers for Blender. Generate valid project files → invoke the real backend. | | **The Rendering Gap** | GUI apps apply effects at render time. If your CLI manipulates project files but uses a naive export tool, effects get silently dropped. Solution: native renderer → filter translation → render script. | | **Filter Translation** | When mapping effects between formats (MLT → ffmpeg), watch for duplicate filter merging, interleaved stream ordering, parameter space differences, and unmappable effects. | | **Timecode Precision** | Non-integer frame rates (29.97fps) cause cumulative rounding. Use `round()` not `int()`, integer arithmetic for display, and ±1 frame tolerance in tests. | | **Output Verification** | Never trust that export worked because it exited 0. Verify: magic bytes, ZIP/OOXML structure, pixel analysis, audio RMS levels, duration checks. | > See the full methodology: [`cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md`](cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md) --- ## 📦 Installation & Usage ### For CLI-Hub Users ```bash # Install the package manager pip install cli-anything-hub # Browse, search, inspect, and install CLIs cli-hub list cli-hub search cli-hub info cli-hub install # Manage installed CLIs cli-hub update cli-hub uninstall cli-hub launch [args...] ``` ### For Plugin Users (Claude Code) ```bash # Add marketplace & install (recommended) /plugin marketplace add HKUDS/CLI-Anything /plugin install cli-anything # Build a CLI for any software with a codebase /cli-anything ``` ### For Generated CLIs ```bash # Install any generated CLI cd /agent-harness pip install -e . # Verify which cli-anything- # Use cli-anything- --help cli-anything- # enters REPL cli-anything- --json # JSON output for agents ``` ### Running Tests ```bash # Run tests for a specific CLI cd /agent-harness python3 -m pytest cli_anything//tests/ -v # Force-installed mode (recommended for validation) CLI_ANYTHING_FORCE_INSTALLED=1 python3 -m pytest cli_anything//tests/ -v -s ``` --- ## 🤝 Contributing We welcome contributions! CLI-Anything is designed to be extensible: - **New software targets** — Use the plugin to generate a CLI for any software with a codebase, then submit your harness via [`cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md`](cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md). - **Methodology improvements** — PRs to `HARNESS.md` that encode new lessons learned - **Plugin enhancements** — New commands, phase improvements, better validation - **Test coverage** — More E2E scenarios, edge cases, workflow tests ### Limitations - **Requires strong foundation models** — CLI-Anything relies on frontier-class models (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4) for reliable harness generation. Weaker or smaller models may produce incomplete or incorrect CLIs that require significant manual correction. - **Relies on available source code** — The 7-phase pipeline analyzes and generates from source code. When the target software only provides compiled binaries that require decompilation, harness quality and coverage will degrade substantially. - **May require iterative refinement** — A single `/cli-anything` run may not fully cover all capabilities. Running `/refine` one or more times is often needed to push the CLI's performance and coverage to production quality. ### Roadmap - [ ] Support for more application categories (CAD, DAW, IDE, EDA, scientific tools) - [ ] Benchmark suite for agent task completion rates - [ ] Community-contributed CLI harnesses for internal/custom software - [ ] Integration with additional agent frameworks beyond Claude Code - [ ] Support packaging APIs for closed-source software and web services into CLIs - [x] Produce SKILL.md alongside the CLI for agent skill discovery and orchestration --- ## 📖 Documentation | Document | Description | |----------|-------------| | [`cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md`](cli-anything-plugin/HARNESS.md) | The methodology SOP — single source of truth | | [`cli-anything-plugin/README.md`](cli-anything-plugin/README.md) | Plugin documentation — commands, options, phases | | [`cli-anything-plugin/QUICKSTART.md`](cli-anything-plugin/QUICKSTART.md) | 5-minute getting started guide | | [`cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md`](cli-anything-plugin/PUBLISHING.md) | Distribution and publishing guide | Each generated harness also includes: - `.md` — Architecture SOP specific to that application - `tests/TEST.md` — Test plan and results documentation --- ## ⭐ Star History If CLI-Anything helps make your software Agent-native, give us a star! ⭐

# ARTEX **Autonomous penetration testing that keeps its receipts.** Self-hosted multi-agent offensive security. A planner explores, workers run real tools, and every finding stays bound to the assets and HTTP traffic that prove it. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/BaaRai/ARTEX?label=release&color=6b34db)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases) [![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](LICENSE) [![CI](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Go](https://img.shields.io/github/go-mod/go-version/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](go.mod) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-join%20the%20server-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/VKyvMTcgXh) [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Screenshots](#screenshots) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#installation) · [Configuration](#configuration) · [Security](SECURITY.md) [![Join us on Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/JOIN%20US%20ON-DISCORD-5865F2?style=for-the-badge&logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/VKyvMTcgXh)
--- ARTEX is a self-hosted, LLM-driven penetration testing platform. It is not a chat wrapper around a scanner: a planner splits a goal into intents, workers execute them with real tools, and the results are written back into **two linked graphs**: one for what you know about the target, one for how the test is progressing. Every finding can carry the captured request and response that justify it, and every autonomous action passes through scope rules, approval gates and budgets. - **It explores, it doesn't chat.** Goal decomposition, intent dispatch, worker execution and write-back form a closed loop that keeps advancing until the goal is proven. - **Two graphs, one audit trail.** The shared asset graph says *what exists*; the per-task exploration graph says *what was tried, what it produced, and why*. Anchors link the two. - **Findings with evidence.** A recording MITM proxy and a browser extension capture real traffic; findings, evidence quotes and retests are tied to the exact request/response. - **Autonomy with brakes.** Human-in-the-loop approvals, argv-prefix rules, scope/deny gates, token and turn budgets, a target noise governor, and prompt-injection framing on tool output. - **Self-hosted and model-agnostic.** One Go binary with the Next.js UI embedded, PostgreSQL, your own Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a local Ollama. --- ## Quick start ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX cp .env.example .env # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (and optionally an LLM key) docker compose up -d --build # builds from this checkout, starts PostgreSQL ``` Open **http://localhost:8787**. On the first visit `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup: ```bash docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token" ``` > Multi-arch release images (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) are published to GitHub Container > Registry at `ghcr.io/baarai/artex` from the next tagged release; v0.7.0 predates the publish > step. For pulling the prebuilt image and all other installation paths (script, binaries, > source, release archives), see [Installation](#installation). --- ## Multi-provider workers In **System → LLM**, configure the profiles you want to use. In **System → Settings**, set the concurrent worker count to at least **2** before starting a task (the count applies to subsequently started tasks). In **System → Agents → Worker**, leave the model set to follow the task; a fixed Worker model takes precedence over rotation. When creating a task, select both profiles in **LLM config chain**, arrange their order, and enable **Enable multi-LLM worker rotation**. For an existing task, open its LLM config control, change the switch or profile order, and save. Rotation assigns successive worker intents A, B, A, B, regardless of completion order. Separate intents can run concurrently on different providers; each intent keeps its selected provider unless it fails over. Planner and other unbound roles continue using the task's current profile. Turning rotation off restores ordered task-level failover. An excluded provider is skipped, so an intent pinned to an exhausted profile falls back to the task's current profile instead of retrying it; rotation keeps cycling the whole list and does not rebalance around a dead provider. Saving the chain resets their failure state. Changes do not interrupt in-flight calls. The rotation cursor starts again after a server restart and saving the chain does not reset it; the profile order and switch remain persisted. The task creation and `PUT /api/tasks/{id}/llm` APIs accept `llm_rotate: true` alongside the ordered `llm_profile_ids`. --- ## How it works ### Dual-graph architecture: exploration graph + asset graph ARTEX separates *what the goals are* from *how far testing has progressed* into two independent graphs linked by anchors: - **Asset graph (shared across tasks).** One source of truth for `root_domain / subdomain / ip / service / app / endpoint`, owned by companies. Parent-child relationships and deduplication keys are computed by the program; agents only submit raw observations. - **Exploration graph (per task).** The task's reasoning and progress: `goal / intent / fact / finding / hint` nodes connected by `spawns / derived_from / yields / proves` edges into a lineage chain. - **Anchors link them.** `exploration_anchors(node_id, asset_id)` ties intents, facts and findings to concrete assets: which assets a direction touched, and which intents tested a given asset. This also powers **asset test coverage** and the coverage graph. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph EG["Exploration graph (per-task · advance chain)"] direction TB G["goal"] I1["intent A"] F1["fact"] I2["intent B"] FD["finding (vulnerability)"] G -->|spawns| I1 I1 -->|yields| F1 F1 -->|derived_from| I2 I2 -->|proves| FD end subgraph AG["Asset graph (globally shared · source of truth)"] direction TB RD["root_domain"] SD["subdomain"] SV["service"] EP["endpoint"] RD --> SD --> SV --> EP end I1 -. anchor .-> SD F1 -. anchor .-> SV I2 -. anchor .-> EP FD -. anchor .-> EP ``` The **planner** reads the exploration graph, judges goals, and dispatches intents only when there is an uncovered direction; a **worker** claims one intent, executes it, writes assets/facts/findings back into both graphs, then stops. ### The engine loop The engine is event-driven: any graph change wakes the planner, workers claim and execute intents, write-back triggers the next round, until `prove_goal` closes the task. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant EV as graph-change debounce participant P as planner participant FR as frontier intent queue participant W as worker participant PX as recording proxy participant DB as dual graphs + activity EV-->>P: wake up P->>DB: read situation (graph_overview prefetch + coverage/scope) P->>FR: dispatch 0..N intents (with asset_ids) Note over P,FR: most wake-ups dispatch 0 (no new direction means done) W->>FR: claimNext claims one intent W->>DB: fetch the raw assets of the intent's asset_ids W->>PX: real tool execution (Kali / Bash / HTTP) PX-->>W: response (fully traced + CA verified) W->>DB: write back fact / asset / finding + per-step activity DB-->>EV: graph change EV-->>P: wake again (closed loop) ``` ### Durable attack chains, shared worker memory Real attack chains are multi-step and ordered (find an injection → get credentials → move laterally). The planner keeps a **todolist retained per task across wake-ups**: it records the chain once, then dispatches the next step only when its prerequisites are satisfied by facts. Workers can also **search each other's execution traces** (`search_all_worker_traces`, `list_worker_traces`, `get_worker_trace`). Observations that never became formal facts (an error message, a response snippet, a hidden parameter) are still reusable by the next worker, while each worker remains confined to the intent it claimed. --- ## Features ### Evidence, not chat logs - **Recording MITM proxy** (`:8788`) with a generated CA: every Bash/HTTP tool call is traced, and request/response evidence can be bound to a finding. - **Browser extension** (`extension/`) for authenticated targets: log in once (captcha, email OTP, 2FA included), capture the session, and the requests/responses land in the same traffic store.
Using the traffic capture extension - Load the unpacked extension from `extension/` (Chrome/Edge: Developer Mode → Load unpacked); - In the popup, set your ARTEX URL and token, then press **Start capture** on the tab you are browsing; - Use the site normally; text requests/responses are batched to `POST /api/traffic/ingest` (authenticated). Binary bodies (images, fonts) are skipped, bodies are truncated at 256 KiB, batches are capped at 50 entries; - Press **Stop** when done. Everything stays in your local traffic store.
- **Verified findings**: findings carry a POE level, a verification status and a note; a finding is `verified` only when a bound proof/response and verbatim evidence quotes support it. Gzip/deflate bodies are decoded before the quote check. The findings table supports bulk status updates, and the report and export show each finding's proof strength next to its status. - **Traffic replay**: open a captured exchange and replay the recorded request (method, URL, headers and stored body) from the traffic detail; replay stays disabled while only the body preview is loaded. - **Vulnerability retest loop**: a dedicated `retester` agent re-runs a finding with optional fixed version/conditions, records `Still reproducible / Fixed / Cannot confirm`, and can move the finding to `Fixed` automatically. Original evidence and reports are preserved. - **Reports and exports**: findings, evidence and task archives, with traffic snapshots kept encrypted at rest. ### Control without slowing down - **Interception gate**: every tool call can require human approval, with rules by `string`, `regex` or **argv prefix**. An argv rule is a JSON array of 1 to 8 tokens (Bash only, for example `["git","push"]`); it matches only a single simple command whose parsed prefix equals the pattern exactly. Pipes, lists, redirections, prefix assignments, subshells, background jobs, wrapper programs and command/parameter substitutions do not match; flags are ignored by construction (`["git","push"]` covers `git push --force`, but `git -C /repo push` matches nothing). Each approval records who decided: `human`, `rule`, `model` or `system`. - **Scope and target gate**: scope rows define the coverage denominator; assets outside the declared scope are not explored. The target gate (off by default, API-only) can refuse destinations that were not approved. - **Budgets**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a whole task (planner and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Near the limit the task enters a forced wrap-up; a worker is not started when the remaining budget cannot cover it. Spend already in `llm_usage` is restored after a restart. A task that is already inside the wrap-up reserve only has that reserve left, so the revived run wraps up instead of starting another worker. The per-worker cost estimate starts again from the defaults (50,000 tokens and 10 turns) until a worker finishes in this process. - **Noise governor**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE=quiet|balanced|aggressive` paces requests ARTEX sends to targets (per-host rate, burst, in-flight limit, jitter, backoff on 429/503, short GET caching). With a profile set, agents also receive low-and-slow flags for the installed scanners. - **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Disable with `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0`. ### Assets and coverage - **Coverage ledger and force-directed coverage graph**: in-scope assets are highlighted as tested or untested, with linked intents, facts and findings per node. - **Company-scoped asset graph**: shared across tasks, deduplicated by the program, with domain → subdomain → service → endpoint containment. - **ScopeSentry sync**: pull asset data from a [ScopeSentry](https://github.com/Autumn-27/ScopeSentry) instance by project or task, merged by company scope into the asset graph for agents to explore.
Syncing from ScopeSentry - On the **Asset Sync** page, enter the ScopeSentry address and API key; - Choose the targets and asset types by **project** or **task** (domains / subdomains / IPs / ports / sites / endpoints…); - Import: rows are merged by company asset scope and become part of the asset graph.
- **Task categories, templates, relations and archives** for repeatable engagements. ### Platform - **LLM profiles with failover**: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible relays and keyless Ollama; multiple profiles per task with automatic failover. - **Token accounting**: per-task and per-session usage, cache reads/writes, and an LLM record view for every call. - **MCP servers, skills, memory and a workspace**: extend the agent with remote tools and reusable prompt/playbook material. - **Web search**: the agent's search tool uses Brave, Tavily or the opt-in Keenable backend, configured in **System → Settings** with the key encrypted at rest; search can also egress through its own proxy. - **Single binary**: the Next.js UI is embedded with `go:embed`; PostgreSQL is the only external dependency. --- ## Installation > Requires **PostgreSQL**; exploration requires an **LLM** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or > `OPENAI_API_KEY`, also configurable in the UI). ### Option 1: one-click install script (recommended) ```bash git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git cd ARTEX ./install.sh ``` The script detects or installs Docker, then offers **① all-Docker** (writes `.env`, runs `docker compose up -d --build`) or **② local build and run** (generates `config.json`, builds the embedded binary, starts it). Unset or empty, the boundary is on; set `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0` (or `false` / `off` / `no`) to disable it. Cost: about 154 bytes per tool result plus one system note. **Noise profile (off by default)**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE` paces the requests ARTEX sends to targets (WebFetch, HTTP custom tools, the enrich probe). Unset or `off` keeps today's behaviour: no limit, no cache. `quiet` = 2 req/s per host (burst 4, 1 in flight), `balanced` = 5 req/s (burst 10, 2 in flight), `aggressive` = 20 req/s (burst 40, 4 in flight). A profile adds jitter, backs off on 429/503 (honours `Retry-After`, bounded retries, GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only), deduplicates identical in-flight GETs and caches them briefly (60/30/10 s; never POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and logs a per-host noise line each minute. `ARTEX_TARGET_USER_AGENT` sets a User-Agent on target requests that carry none. With traffic capture on, Bash commands that use the proxy (curl, wget, python-requests) are paced too, per host by the same rate and jitter, and counted in the same per-host lines. The in-flight caps, retries and cache apply only to ARTEX's own requests. This is best effort, not a security boundary. Raw scanners such as nmap are not paced, and neither is a command that bypasses the proxy (`--noproxy`, a removed proxy variable). With capture off, nothing launched from Bash is paced. The low-and-slow prompt block supplies the rate flags in every case. The **Target noise** card in System settings sets the profile at runtime (no restart) and shows the per-host counters; once saved, that setting takes precedence over `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE`. **Scanner User-Agent (opt-in per task)** adds a stable ARTEX User-Agent to supported target requests so defenders can correlate them with an approved assessment. See the [configuration and WAF triage guide](docs/scanner-user-agent.md). **Low-and-slow agent guidance (off by default)**: when a noise profile is set, the planner, worker, main agent and chat agents receive a code-owned prompt block with the profile's per-host limits and exact rate/delay flags for the installed scanners. It tells them to test one host at a time, back off on 429/503 and never raise the rate to meet a deadline. **Run budgets (off by default)**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a task's total spend (planner rounds and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Unset or `0` means unlimited. A worker is not started when the remaining task budget cannot cover its estimated cost (the average of finished workers, else 50,000 tokens and 10 turns). Near the wrap-up reserve (the larger of 5% and 20,000 tokens, and 2 turns) the task enters a forced wrap-up: the planner writes a summary and final goal judgment, and workers may only write back. The task then ends `done` if its goals are met, else `timeout`. Practical floor: below 50,000 tokens no worker starts; 50,000-70,000 typically gives one worker then wrap-up; pick well above 70,000 for real exploration. Planner, worker, judge, and compactor rows in `llm_usage` are counted back into the cap when a ledger is created, including after a restart and after a revived run drops its ledger. A restored task already inside the wrap-up reserve does not get another worker: only that reserve remains, and the run wraps up. Chat, goal decomposition, and side questions are stored on the same task and are not counted. The per-worker average is not restored (usage rows have no run boundary), so the estimate starts from the defaults until a worker finishes in this process. **Common flags**: `./start.sh -addr :8787 -proxy :8788` (`-addr` frontend/API, `-proxy` traffic recording proxy). ### External PostgreSQL ARTEX already supports an external PostgreSQL 16+ instance — the `postgres` service in `docker-compose.yml` is only the bundled default. Because the database is startup configuration and the system's single source of truth, there is no runtime database switcher in the UI: change the environment variables and restart the server to point at another instance. Configure the connection with either a full connection string or individual parts: - **`ARTEX_PG_DSN`**: full PostgreSQL connection URL (for example `postgres://artex:pass@db.example.internal:5432/artex?sslmode=require`). When set, it takes precedence over the `ARTEX_PG_*` variables and you are responsible for percent-encoding any URL-special characters in the username or password. - **`ARTEX_PG_*` parts** (recommended when passwords contain `/`, `?`, `%`, `@`, `:`, or spaces — ARTEX percent-encodes the user and password and removes `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` from the environment at startup): - `ARTEX_PG_HOST` — PostgreSQL host - `ARTEX_PG_PORT` — PostgreSQL port (default `5432`) - `ARTEX_PG_USER` — database user - `ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD` — database password (raw, not URL-encoded) - `ARTEX_PG_DBNAME` — database name - `ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE` — TLS mode (`disable`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`) #### Compose without the bundled `postgres` service To run ARTEX against an external PostgreSQL server with Docker Compose, remove the `postgres` service, the `depends_on` block, and the `pgdata` volume from `docker-compose.yml`, and point `artex` at your database: ```yaml services: artex: image: ghcr.io/baarai/artex:latest security_opt: - "no-new-privileges:true" environment: # Option A: individual parts (recommended; percent-encodes special characters) ARTEX_PG_HOST: ${ARTEX_PG_HOST:?Set ARTEX_PG_HOST in .env} ARTEX_PG_PORT: ${ARTEX_PG_PORT:-5432} ARTEX_PG_USER: ${ARTEX_PG_USER:-artex} ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD: ${ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD:?Set ARTEX_PG_PASSWORD in .env} ARTEX_PG_DBNAME: ${ARTEX_PG_DBNAME:-artex} ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE: ${ARTEX_PG_SSLMODE:-require} # Option B: full DSN (overrides ARTEX_PG_* when set) # ARTEX_PG_DSN: ${ARTEX_PG_DSN} ARTEX_JWT_KEY_DIR: /app/keys ports: - "${ARTEX_BIND_ADDR:-127.0.0.1}:8787:8787" - "127.0.0.1:8788:8788" volumes: - ./data:/app/data - ./keys:/app/keys restart: unless-stopped ``` #### Local disk usage (`data/`) Moving PostgreSQL to an external host does **not** move the runtime `data/` directory off local disk. `data/` still stores spilled HTTP/TCP traffic blobs (`data/traffic/_blobs`), LLM transcripts, task working files, and local task archives, so heavy workloads can still fill the host disk if `data/` is on a small volume. Mount `data/` on a suitably sized volume, and consider setting `ARTEX_ARCHIVE_STORAGE=s3` (see [Task archive storage](docs/task-archive-storage.md)) to offload cold task archives to object storage. ### Reverse proxy deployment (HTTPS / exposing only 443) The frontend, API and SSE stream share port 8787 (the binary listens on `127.0.0.1:8787` by default; the Docker container publishes on `127.0.0.1`), and the activity stream is same-origin by default, so **no `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` is needed**: expose 443 and keep 8787 internal. SSE keeps a long-lived connection with continuous pushes, so the proxy **must disable buffering**; otherwise the browser connects but never receives events. Redirect plain HTTP first, so a bookmarked `http://` URL never reaches the app unencrypted: ```nginx server { listen 80; server_name your.domain.com; return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } ``` Then the TLS server: ```nginx server { listen 443 ssl; server_name your.domain.com; # ssl_certificate / ssl_certificate_key ... location / { # 512 MiB combined file limit plus 1 MiB of multipart metadata. client_max_body_size 513m; proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; # SSE essentials: buffering off, long timeouts, HTTP/1.1 proxy_buffering off; proxy_cache off; proxy_read_timeout 3600s; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; } } ``` **Login rate limit behind a proxy**: login allows 10 attempts per minute per client IP. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so without further setup all users share one budget and an attacker who fails 10 logins blocks everyone, admin included, for up to 15 minutes. Keep the `X-Forwarded-For` line and set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (comma-separated CIDRs, empty by default) to the address ARTEX sees the proxy connect from: - **nginx and ARTEX both on the host** (binary, `./start.sh`): the peer is `127.0.0.1`; start ARTEX with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1/32`. - **nginx on the host, ARTEX in Docker** (`docker-compose.yml`): the connection reaches the container from the Docker bridge gateway (a `172.x` address), not from `127.0.0.1`. Find it with `docker network inspect artex_default --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}'` (the network is `_default`), put `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=/32` in `.env`, then `docker compose up -d`. For a peer in that list, ARTEX reads `X-Forwarded-For` from the right and takes the first address that is not a trusted proxy; from any other peer the header is ignored. Trust only proxies you run: a trusted peer can claim any client address. **Security headers**: every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a same-origin referrer policy and a `frame-ancestors 'self'` CSP; console documents additionally get a `Permissions-Policy` and COOP/CORP. `Strict-Transport-Security` is sent only when the request is known to be HTTPS: directly over TLS, or via `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` from a trusted proxy. The same list above enables it, so with nginx in front, the 443 server answers with HSTS after you set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES`. > Only when SSE needs a different origin from the page (e.g. a dedicated subdomain) should you set > `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` **at build time** (it is baked into the static bundle during `next build`; > setting it at container runtime has no effect). --- ## Operations ### Troubleshooting an empty tool call In the task's session transcript, expand the affected tool call and compare **Command** and **Output**. The `UNTRUSTED_OUTPUT` markers identify the boundary around tool output. They are expected and should stay enabled while troubleshooting. - **Command shows `{}`.** The recorded tool input is an empty JSON object. For a tool that requires a command, this means its command argument was missing. Check which model and version produced the call. - **Command shows `(empty)` or `(failed to load)`.** The transcript has no input detail to display or could not fetch it. If the session record contains a command, include that discrepancy in a report. - **Output shows `[]`.** This is the recorded result body. Check the row's success or failure indicator and its input separately before drawing conclusions about what ran. For a recurring problem, share the ARTEX version or commit, the model and version, and a sanitized excerpt of the affected input and result. Remove credentials, target data, and other sensitive content before sharing. ### Backups `scripts/backup.sh` dumps the Postgres database (and optionally the data directory) with timestamped output and rotation: ```bash scripts/backup.sh --with-data # db dump + data/ archive, keep 14 scripts/backup.sh --keep 7 # db only, keep 7 ``` Restore into a running stack: ```bash gunzip -c backups/artex-db-.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T postgres \ psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" ``` Stored secrets (LLM API keys, proxies and gateway custom headers, MCP env, task credentials, notification channel config, Brave/Tavily search keys, web search and global proxies, the execution spec of custom tools, the capture-proxy rewrite rules) are encrypted in the database with the key in `keys/secret.key` (generated at first start, mode 0600, next to `jwt.key`). **A database backup without that key cannot restore those secrets**: back up `keys/` with the dump, separately. Deployments without a persistent disk set `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY` (32 bytes, base64 or hex, e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`). ARTEX refuses to start when the database holds encrypted secrets and no key is available. Daily cron example (03:20, operator crontab): ``` 20 3 * * * cd /path/to/ARTEX && scripts/backup.sh --with-data >> backups/backup.log 2>&1 ``` ### Updating and upgrading > Upgrading swaps the program and never touches data: the Postgres volume `pgdata`, `./data` > (traffic index, task files, transcripts), `./keys` (`jwt.key`, `secret.key`) and `./skills` are > preserved. **No manual database step is needed**: on every start ARTEX applies its embedded > `schema.sql` baseline, then any pending numbered migration from `db/migrations/`, in order, each > in its own transaction. Restarting the new binary is the upgrade. Back up `./data`, `keys/` and > the database before upgrading. **Update banner (opt-in, off by default)**: start ARTEX with `ARTEX_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to ask the public GitHub releases API for the latest tag, at most once per 24 hours (cached in memory; a failed check is not retried within that window). When the release is newer, the web UI shows a dismissible strip linking to Releases. The request sends only `User-Agent: artex-update-check`. Unset, ARTEX makes no update request and shows no banner. #### Upgrading from a clone made before 2026-10-23 The repository history was rewritten that day to drop a personal email address from the commit metadata.
